key_facts: **IPL** uses filtered broad-spectrum flashlamp light to target **melanin** (lentigines, hair) and **haemoglobin** (redness, telangiectasia).
Usually 3–6 sessions; treated pigment darkens ('coffee grounds') then flakes over 1–2 weeks.
Risks: burns, blistering, hypo- or hyperpigmentation, scarring, eye injury; highest in tanned or darker skin.
Never treat undiagnosed pigmented lesions; caution with photosensitising drugs, recent isotretinoin, HSV.
Melasma is a poor candidate; cosmetic and not NHS-funded.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Intense pulsed light (IPL)** is a non-laser flashlamp delivering broad-spectrum light through filters to treat vascular redness, solar lentigines and unwanted dark hair, with modest texture benefit.

ul: Selective photothermolysis: melanin and oxyhaemoglobin absorb the light and heat up; dermal heating may remodel collagen modestly.
Darker or tanned skin absorbs more epidermal energy, giving a higher risk of burns and pigment change.
**"IPL is a laser"**: it is non-coherent broad-spectrum light, less selective than lasers.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: IPL heats **coloured targets** in the skin, which absorb the light more than their surroundings.

mech.t: Melanin and oxyhaemoglobin absorb specific wavelengths.
Short pulses heat the target faster than heat spreads (selective photothermolysis).
Damaged pigment is shed; heated vessels collapse and are reabsorbed.
Epidermal melanin also absorbs energy, so tanned or darker skin burns more easily.

ul: Sessions often 3–6, weeks apart; treated pigment darkens like “coffee grounds” then flakes over 1–2 weeks.
Adverse effects: burns, blistering, **hypo-/hyperpigmentation** (sometimes grid footprints), scarring, paradoxical hair growth, eye injury.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Before IPL: confirm the diagnosis of every pigmented spot (no undiagnosed lesions), Fitzpatrick type, recent tan, photosensitising drugs and HSV history. Melasma is generally a poor IPL candidate.

ul: Check practitioner training, insurance, patch test and (in Wales) HIW registration for Class 3B/4 lasers/IPL in independent clinics.

Contraindications/cautions: undiagnosed pigmented lesions, active infection/HSV, recent tan, photosensitivity disorders, many photosensitising drugs; extra caution in skin types IV–VI and on isotretinoin (many delay treatment).
Aftercare: SPF, gentle skincare, no picking; seek review for blistering or infection.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Eye pain or visual change during/after IPL: **urgent ophthalmology**.
Blistering burns or striped hypopigmentation: stop further treatment; specialist wound/pigment advice.
Undiagnosed changing pigmented lesion: cancel IPL; refer.
Burns, pigment change (grid pattern), scarring, eye injury, paradoxical hair growth.
Results fade with new sun damage; maintenance sessions are common.

pearls: IPL is versatile but unforgiving on tanned or darker skin without expert settings.
Coffee-ground darkening is expected; picking prolongs marks.

quiz.q: Who is at higher risk of IPL burns and pigment change?
Is melasma a good IPL indication?
quiz.a: Generally no; heat can worsen it.
Expected darkening of treated pigment that flakes off over 1–2 weeks.
